description:
Here's the version rewritten for a team:

"We're a team of passionate students with experience in Python, UI design, and project management, and we love building user-friendly solutions to real everyday problems. We're aiming for a project that's both innovative and practical, and we want teammates who share our drive to learn fast and create something we're proud of.
summary: AstroPulse is a web app that helps astronauts monitor their own health during long space missions, and lets Mission Control watch the whole crew at once. In a 30-second daily check-in, astronauts log nine health indicators: resting heart rate, blood pressure, blood glucose, body temperature, blood oxygen, sleep, mood, body mass and daily radiation dose. AstroPulse compares each reading with clinical ranges and NASA limits, then gives a health score from 0 to 100, a status (nominal, caution or critical) and clear alerts that say what changed and what to do. Every alert is linked to NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight, so crews learn why space causes the problem. It adapts to five environments, from the space station to a Mars base, and tracks each astronaut's career radiation against NASA's limit. On missions to the Moon and Mars, where help from Earth is far away, AstroPulse helps crews catch problems early and act on their own.
details:
Try it live: https://astropulse-7v3l.onrender.com

Choose an astronaut and enter PIN 111111 to 666666 (one per crew member). The first load can take up to a minute while the free server wakes up. All crew health data is simulated; no real medical data is used.

WHAT IT DOES

- Health check-in: astronauts log 9 indicators (resting heart rate, blood pressure, blood glucose, body temperature, SpO2, sleep, mood, body mass, daily radiation dose) and can upload health images such as skin or eye photos.

- Dashboard: a health score from 0 to 100, a status (nominal, caution or critical) and plain-language alerts that explain what changed and what to do next.

- Body map: shows which body systems are affected and the countermeasures for each.

- Trends: charts of every indicator over time against its normal range, so slow changes like weight loss or rising blood pressure stand out.

- Five environments: space station, deep-space spacecraft, pressurized rover, lunar base and Mars base, each with its own gravity, communication delay, radiation level and evacuation time.

- Career radiation: each astronaut's lifetime dose is tracked against NASA's 600 mSv career limit, with warnings at 50% and 80%.

- Quests: 11 daily healthy-habit tasks (exercise, sleep, hydration, window time and more) that earn XP, ranks and 10 badges.

- Health Guide: explains every indicator, NASA's five hazards, 17 NASA risks of human spaceflight (marked by what AstroPulse tracks), the five environments, and 15 linked sources.

- Mission Control: one screen with every crew member's score, status and alerts.

HOW IT WORKS

The frontend is React with Vite, Framer Motion animations and Recharts charts. The backend is a Python FastAPI service with a PostgreSQL database. A health engine on the server checks every reading, builds the score and alerts, and adds up mission and career radiation. The live version runs on Render (website and API) and Neon (PostgreSQL).

Medical data is private by design. Astronaut PINs and the admin password are stored only as bcrypt hashes. Astronauts can see only their own records, and the server enforces this. In an emergency, a crewmate can open another astronaut's record read-only for 60 minutes with a stated reason; every access is logged and the astronaut is told. Health images are never public.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

On missions to the Moon and Mars, help from Earth is minutes to months away. AstroPulse gives each crew member an early warning system they can use alone, in under a minute a day, and it teaches as it warns. The same approach can help people in remote places on Earth, such as Antarctic stations, ships and remote clinics.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

AstroPulse joins three things that are usually separate: health tracking, education about NASA's five hazards, and game-style quests that reward healthy habits. Alerts change with the environment: the same radiation dose means something different on the station than on Mars.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Scientific validity (ranges and limits from NASA standards, NASA's Human Research Program, the Canadian Space Agency and published studies, each linked in the app), privacy of medical data, ease of use for a busy astronaut, and communication delays far from Earth.

NEXT STEPS

Connect wearable sensors instead of typed readings, and add full offline use for long communication delays.

AI USE

The code, the simulated demo data and parts of the text were created with help from Claude (Anthropic), an AI assistant. Our team chose the features, tested the app, checked the sources and made the final decisions.

TOOLS

React, Vite, Framer Motion, Recharts, Lucide icons, Python, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, PostgreSQL, bcrypt, PyJWT, Render, Neon, GitHub, Claude.
